svg.aria-label: Lemma 5: forcing the recovered tail to the value i pins the padding length, so exactly one candidate byte completes the pattern and the sweep returns true once
svg.text: Lemma 5: at iteration i the answer is unique, so one sweep settles the byte
Shown for i = 3, with P*[13 .. 15] already recovered and forced to the value i.

text.font-family: STIX Two Math, Latin Modern Math, Cambria Math, Times New Roman, serif

svg.text: the last byte is pinned to i, so step 3 reads p = i
the only byte still free: Δ[15 − i]
Why exactly one value works
step 3 reads p from the last byte, and that byte is i
so well-formedness asks: are the last i + 1 bytes all equal to i ?
bytes 16 − i … 15 already are, by the induction hypothesis
so the whole test reduces to: is byte 15 − i equal to i ?
one value of Δ[15 − i] does that, namely P*[15 − i] ⊕ i
so the sweep returns true exactly once
the sweep over Δ[15 − i]
FF
the one true
At most 2⁸ probes, and the true one names the byte:

text.font-family: STIX Two Math, Latin Modern Math, Cambria Math, Times New Roman, serif

svg.text: This is why Phase 2 needs no disambiguation step
Phase 1
The last byte is itself being searched, so p may be
anything in [1, 43]: several runs can answer true,
and Phase 1b is needed to tell them apart.
Phase 2
The last byte is pinned to i, so p = i is pinned too.
Only one run length is even in question, and only one
byte value completes it. No ambiguity arises.
Each iteration is exact, so nothing accumulates: Lemma 4 fixes two bytes, then 14 exact iterations fix the rest, and
the conditioning in the statement is discharged by the iteration before it.
